meta.title: GDPR records of processing (ROPA): what Art. 30 requires
meta.description: What goes into a record of processing activities, when the under-250 exemption applies, and what the NIS2 walkthrough already records for it.

ropa.title: Creating a record of processing activities: what Art. 30 GDPR requires
ropa.subtitle: The record of processing activities (ROPA) describes every processing of personal data in your company: purpose, data subjects, categories of data, recipients, third countries and, where possible, erasure time limits and TOMs (Art. 30(1) GDPR). In the view of Germany's data protection conference, the exemption for fewer than 250 employees rarely applies.

sections.heading: What goes into a record of processing activities?
paragraphs: Each controller maintains a record of all processing activities under its responsibility (Art. 30(1) GDPR). The controller is your company, because it determines the purposes and means of the processing (Art. 4(7)).

It gives the name and contact details of your company and of any data protection officer. For each activity it states the purposes, the categories of data subjects and of personal data, and the categories of recipients. It adds transfers to third countries, naming the country, and, where possible, the time limits for erasure and a general description of the TOMs under Art. 32(1).

The record is kept in writing, which includes electronic form (Art. 30(3)). You make it available to the supervisory authority on request (Art. 30(4)); you do not have to publish it. If your company itself processes data on behalf of others, it keeps a second record for that under Art. 30(2).

sections.heading: Does the duty apply under 250 employees?
paragraphs: Art. 30(5) exempts organisations employing fewer than 250 persons “unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or the processing includes special categories of data”, such as health data, or data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

One of these conditions is enough. The DSK is the conference of Germany's federal and state data protection authorities. It names payroll and customer data management as processing that is not occasional, and it expects the exemption to apply only rarely.

On that reading, a company that runs payroll or maintains customer data regularly is not exempt. The German wording of paragraph 5 was corrected in 2016 (OJ L 314, 22.11.2016), so German quotes of the original version word the exemption differently.

sections.heading: What is a processing activity? An example
paragraphs: The DSK generally treats a processing activity as a business process at a suitable level of abstraction. Each new purpose is a separate activity. Name it after its purpose, such as “payroll and salary accounting”. For the software, the DSK template has an optional field, “Name des eingesetzten Verfahrens” (name of the procedure used).

A made-up example: Muster Metall GmbH has 80 employees. Its entry “payroll” gives the purpose as paying wages, the data subjects as employees, and the data as master data, bank details and tax attributes. Recipients are the tax office, social insurance bodies and banks, plus the payroll software vendor where it processes the data in its cloud.

Under third countries it says “none”, because the DSK advises stating that explicitly too. The erasure time limit names the legal provision and when the period starts. For TOMs, the entry refers to the cryptography policy and the staff, access and asset policy from the NIS 2 walkthrough. The DSK expressly allows such references to information security documents.

sections.heading: Which mistakes to avoid in the record
paragraphs: A record that only lists software, such as “Microsoft 365” or “DATEV”, describes tools instead of purposes. One program often serves several activities, and one activity often uses several programs.

An entry such as “statutory retention periods” is a general reference, and in the DSK's view that is not enough: it asks for precise information. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) recommends in its February 2026 report that the record state whether a legal obligation to retain the data exists.
A record goes out of date with every new program and every new service provider. The DSK recommends documenting changes and keeping that documentation for one year.

sections.heading: With an AI assistant: what it can prepare for the record
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot can draft entries from your own documents: the list of your processes and software, your supplier list and your contracts. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard, it also reads the lists in the NIS 2 walkthrough. That covers the areas assigned to the person who connected it.

Anything your documents do not state, such as a legal basis or an erasure time limit, is a suggestion in the draft. Whether an entry is correct and which time limit applies is for your company to decide as controller, with your data protection officer where one is designated.

Whatever you hand the assistant, such as payroll lists, its vendor processes too. Where the vendor acts as a processor, a contract under Art. 28(3) GDPR is required. A GDPR walkthrough on nisd2.eu is in the works, with the same MCP server as the NIS 2 walkthrough.
A request to the assistant can read like this:
sections.code: Use get_walkthrough to read items 2.2 and 5.1. For every ticked process that involves personal data, draft an entry for the record of processing activities under Art. 30(1) GDPR, with purpose, data subjects, categories of data, recipients, third country, erasure time limit and TOMs. Flag every field the records do not state and leave it empty. Do not enter anything in the walkthrough.

walk.heading: What the NIS 2 walkthrough already records
walk.lead: Item 2.2 records processes, software and their vendors: in our reading, source material for the record, but not a record under Art. 30 GDPR.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has, screen “What your company does every day”: the processes you tick, such as “HR and payroll administration”. Each process involving personal data becomes one or more processing activities. The walkthrough does not ask for purposes, categories of data or erasure time limits.

2.2, “Software for customers, staff and money” and “Which software exactly, and from whom?”: each program with its vendor, such as the payroll software. That fits the optional field “Name des eingesetzten Verfahrens” in the DSK template. Whether a vendor processes data on your behalf or moves it to a third country is not recorded there.

On the “Export” page, “Everything in one document” contains the sections “Assets” and “Suppliers”. Admins, reviewers and management save it as a PDF and pass it to whoever handles your data protection.

That person adds purpose, data subjects, categories of data, recipients, third country, erasure time limit and TOMs per activity. If the list in 2.2 changes, the record does not change with it: compare the two whenever a program is added.
walk.seeItAlt: Item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough, screen “What your company does every day”: under “Business processes” 12 of 14 processes are ticked, among them “Sales and customer service”, “HR and payroll administration” and “Finance and accounting”
walk.next: Record your processes in the walkthrough

items.q: Is there a template for the record of processing activities?
items.a: Yes. The DSK publishes a template for controllers under Art. 30(1) GDPR on datenschutzkonferenz-online.de, dated February 2018, with notes on filling it in. It is in German and has a cover sheet for your company's details and one form per processing activity with the required information.

items.q: Who has to keep the record of processing activities?
items.a: The controller, meaning your company (Art. 30(1)). A data protection officer informs, advises and monitors compliance (Art. 39(1)). They can look after the record, but the duty stays with the company; decide internally who maintains it.

items.q: Is a NIS 2 asset list the same as a record of processing activities?
items.a: No. The list in 2.2 says what your company works with, so you can protect it. The Art. 30 record describes, per purpose, whose data you process, where it goes and when it is erased. One list helps you build the other.

items.q: How often should the record of processing activities be updated?
items.a: Art. 30 sets no interval. The record covers all processing activities under your responsibility, which includes new ones. Update it whenever a new purpose, program or service provider comes in, and document the change.

meta.title: GDPR TOMs: technical and organisational measures
meta.description: What Art. 32 GDPR asks of your TOMs, how to choose and describe appropriate measures, and which records in the NIS2 walkthrough already cover part of it.

toms.title: GDPR TOMs: technical and organisational measures under Art. 32
toms.subtitle: TOMs are the technical and organisational measures you use to protect personal data, such as encryption, access rights, backups and rules for staff. Art. 32 GDPR requires a level of security appropriate to the risk for the people concerned. The law prescribes no fixed list.

sections.heading: What does Art. 32 GDPR require?
paragraphs: Controllers and processors implement appropriate technical and organisational measures “to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk” (Art. 32(1)). They take into account the state of the art, the costs, the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the likelihood and severity of the risk for the rights and freedoms of people.

The measures include “inter alia as appropriate”: pseudonymisation and encryption (point (a)), the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems (b), timely restoration after an incident (c), and a process for regularly testing the effectiveness (d). In the German text, the word “gegebenenfalls” (as appropriate) was added by a correction in 2018.

In the assessment, destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure and unauthorised access weigh in particular (para. 2). Para. 4 also requires steps to ensure that staff with access to personal data process it only on instructions.

sections.heading: How do you choose appropriate measures?
paragraphs: The yardstick is the risk to the people whose data you process. The DSK is the conference of Germany's data protection authorities. In its Kurzpapier Nr. 18 it describes the risk with two dimensions: the severity of possible harm, such as damage to reputation or financial loss, and the likelihood that it occurs.

The DSK sorts the result into low risk, risk and high risk. Where a high risk is likely, its notes on the record of processing say you determine the measures as part of a data protection impact assessment under Art. 35.

For choosing measures, the same notes refer to the DSK's Standard Data Protection Model (SDM), to the BSI's IT-Grundschutz and to ISO standards. SDM version 3.1 of 2024 maps measures to seven protection goals, from data minimisation to intervenability, meaning that data subjects can exercise their rights. It reads these goals from the data subject's point of view.

sections.heading: Where and how to describe your TOMs
paragraphs: Art. 32 prescribes no separate document. The record of processing activities should, however, contain a general description of the measures where possible (Art. 30(1)(g)), and in the DSK's view that description is the rule despite “where possible”.

It should be concrete enough for the supervisory authority to make a first assessment of lawfulness (DSK, Kurzpapier Nr. 1). You may refer to existing documents, such as a security concept from your information security work, and then add what applies to a particular processing.

Art. 32 applies to processors too, and your company uses only processors that provide sufficient guarantees (Art. 28(1)). The contract binds them to all measures required under Art. 32 and to giving you the information needed to demonstrate compliance (Art. 28(3)(c) and (h)). Ask for their description before you engage them.

sections.heading: Example: the TOMs of a company with 80 employees
paragraphs: Muster Metall GmbH, a made-up company, describes its TOMs along the points of Art. 32(1). A weak sentence would be: “We protect data in line with the state of the art.” It says nothing about what actually happens.

Its description says instead: the disks of all laptops are encrypted, and the recovery key is kept apart from the device (a). Rights are assigned through roles, and email and remote access require a second factor (b). The server is backed up daily, and the date of the last restore that worked is recorded (c).
For point (d) it states who reviews the measures and when: management together with the external data protection officer. The company does not use pseudonymisation so far and records why.

sections.heading: Which mistakes to avoid with TOMs
paragraphs: Do not copy a template unchanged. It describes measures that may not apply in your business, and your company must be able to demonstrate what it actually does (Art. 5(2)).
Do not list only technology. Organisational measures include binding staff to confidentiality, instructions to staff under Art. 32(4) and a concept for roles and access rights.
Do not forget point (d). Without a process that tests effectiveness, the description is a snapshot of one day. Art. 24(1) requires measures to be reviewed and updated where necessary.
Do not take over NIS 2 measures unchecked. They protect your systems, while Art. 32 asks about the risk to the people whose data you process.

sections.heading: With an AI assistant: what it can draft for your TOMs
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot can draft a description along points (a) to (d) from your documents and flag gaps, such as missing information on pseudonymisation. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard, it can also read your NIS 2 walkthrough. Our article on drafting TOMs with AI from your NIS 2 records shows how.
Whether a measure is appropriate to the risk is for your company to decide as controller (Art. 32(1)). Check every sentence of the draft against what is actually set up in your business.

If you give the assistant documents containing personal data, its vendor processes them too. Where the vendor acts as a processor, a contract under Art. 28(3) GDPR is required. A GDPR walkthrough on nisd2.eu is in the works, with the same MCP server as the NIS 2 walkthrough.

walk.heading: What the NIS 2 walkthrough already records
walk.lead: The complete documentation from the export holds policies your Art. 32 description can refer to; you keep the description itself separately.
points: On the “Export” page, admins, reviewers and management open “Everything in one document”. That is the complete documentation with its as-of date, which you file with “Save as PDF”.

Under “Documents” it prints the full text of the policies you wrote in the walkthrough, among them the cryptography policy from 9.1, the staff, access and asset policy from 10.1 and the business continuity plan from 4.2.
Your description can refer to this PDF, as the DSK provides for. According to the DSK's notes, any document you refer to also goes to the supervisory authority on request.

Which item fits which point of Art. 32(1) is set out, in our own mapping, in the article on drafting TOMs with AI from your NIS 2 records. The walkthrough does not ask about the risk to the people concerned or about pseudonymisation; your company adds those.
walk.seeItAlt: The “Complete documentation” from the export, headed “NIS 2 documentation”, with a sample company's details, the contents from “Implementation status” to “Answers by area”, and the “Save as PDF” button at the top

items.q: Which TOMs are mandatory?
items.a: There is no fixed list. Art. 32(1) gives examples that apply “as appropriate” and requires a level of security appropriate to the risk. Which measures that means depends on your processing; record why you do not use a measure the article names.

items.q: What is the difference between technical and organisational measures?
items.a: Technical measures work in devices and software, such as encryption, backups or a second factor at sign-in. Organisational measures govern what people do: roles and rights, confidentiality obligations, instructions and training. Art. 32 requires both.

items.q: Is there a checklist for TOMs?
items.a: In its notes on the record of processing activities (February 2018, in German), the DSK lists typical measures for each area of Art. 32(1), from pseudonymisation to an emergency concept. It opens each list with “u. a.” (among others), so the lists are examples. Use them as a checklist and write down what applies in your company.

items.q: How often do TOMs have to be reviewed?
items.a: The GDPR sets no fixed interval. Art. 32(1)(d) requires a process for regularly testing effectiveness, and Art. 24(1) requires review and updating “where necessary”. Set the interval yourself, review as well whenever a new processing or a new program comes in, and record the date and the result.

meta.title: GDPR deletion concept and retention policy: what it covers
meta.description: What a deletion concept under Art. 17 GDPR must settle: time limit, start and owner per type of data, backups, and what the NIS2 walkthrough records.

erasure.title: GDPR deletion concept: what it must settle
erasure.subtitle: A deletion concept (a retention and deletion policy) sets, for each type of personal data, how long it stays, when the period starts, who deletes it and how. It puts two duties into practice: keeping data no longer than necessary (Art. 5(1)(e) GDPR) and erasing it without undue delay when Art. 17 applies. Backups are included.

sections.heading: Which duties sit behind a deletion concept?
paragraphs: The GDPR does not use the term, but the duties behind it are there. Personal data may be kept in a form that permits identification “for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed” (Art. 5(1)(e)).

Art. 17(1) obliges your company to erase data without undue delay where one of the listed grounds applies, for example when the data is no longer necessary for its purpose or consent has been withdrawn. That applies on request and, as the German Data Protection Conference (DSK) writes in its Kurzpapier Nr. 11, without one too.

Art. 17(3) lists exceptions, such as a legal obligation to retain the data (point (b)) or the defence of legal claims (point (e)). In the DSK's view, these do not allow unlimited storage either: once their purpose is met, the data is erased.

sections.heading: What a deletion concept must settle
paragraphs: At its core it is one deletion rule per type of data: the time limit, the event that starts it, and the basis for it. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) names as a good practice of some controllers a table that brings together type of data, legal basis and retention period.

The DSK's Standard Data Protection Model (SDM) covers deletion in its building block 60. Under it, you settle who checks, orders and carries out deletions. It expressly lists quick formatting and a mere promise not to use the data any more as not enough.

According to the SDM, a piece of data is erased only once no copy remains with you or a processor. Processors delete or return the data at the end of the service and delete existing copies (Art. 28(3)(g)). You tell recipients about each erasure unless that proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort (Art. 19).

sections.heading: What applies to backups?
paragraphs: A backup is a copy. According to SDM building block 60, the duty to erase in principle covers backup copies too, though not necessarily at the same moment as in the live system. If deleting safely in the backup would take so long that it coincides with the scheduled overwrite anyway, it can happen then.

The rule that matters most concerns restores. When your IT restores data from a backup, data already erased comes back. The SDM requires that it be erased again immediately afterwards, and processes that monitor this.

The EDPB does not consider it always advisable to modify backups, because they protect against attacks such as ransomware. In that case, its February 2026 report says, you need a procedure that keeps track of erasure requests and applies them to restored systems. Half of the responding supervisory authorities raised concerns about deletion in backups.

So your deletion concept states, for each backup system, how long copies are kept, and keeps a list of erasures that is worked through again after a restore. The list names which record is to be erased, for example by a customer number. For documentation of erasures, the SDM requires that it contain no content data that has to be erased.

sections.heading: Example: one deletion rule and one restore
paragraphs: Muster Metall GmbH, a made-up company with 80 employees, keeps correspondence on orders as commercial letters for six years under the German Commercial Code (§ 257(1) and (4) HGB). The period starts at the end of the calendar year in which the letter was received or sent (para. 5). An email from March 2026 therefore stays until the end of 2032.

In the example, its daily backup is kept for 30 days. After an attack, its IT restores the state from two weeks earlier. Before the restart it works through that fortnight's erasure list again; it holds, for example, the customer number of a customer who had withdrawn her consent to the newsletter, and her address is erased again afterwards.

sections.heading: Which mistakes to avoid in a deletion concept
paragraphs: Do not set one time limit for everything just because it sounds safe. Data without a retention duty then stays too long, and in the DSK's view a general reference to retention duties is not enough.

Do not delete only in the main system. Copies can also sit in mailboxes, on mobile devices and in cloud services; the SDM requires processes that catch every copy. For retired devices, item 10.1 of the NIS 2 walkthrough provides for secure wiping or destruction.
Retaining is not continuing to use. The exception in Art. 17(3)(b) applies only “to the extent that” processing is necessary for the legal obligation.

sections.heading: With an AI assistant: what it can prepare for the deletion concept
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot can build a table of all types of data from your record of processing activities and propose a deletion rule for each. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard, it also reads what the NIS 2 walkthrough records about your backup systems.

Check every proposed time limit in the current statute. § 257(4) HGB, for example, has applied in a new version since 1 January 2025 and gives eight years for accounting vouchers. Which time limit applies is for your company to decide as controller.

Erasure lists can contain personal data, which the assistant's vendor then processes too. Where the vendor acts as a processor, a contract under Art. 28(3) GDPR is required. A GDPR walkthrough on nisd2.eu is in the works, with the same MCP server as the NIS 2 walkthrough.

walk.heading: What the NIS 2 walkthrough already records
walk.lead: Item 4.4 records your backup systems; it does not ask how long copies are kept or what happens to erased data after a restore.
points: On the walkthrough's path, 4.4 Record your backups comes further down, straight after 4.2 Write the business continuity plan. In 4.4 you enter, per backup system, how often it backs up and when a restore from it last worked. In your deletion concept, add for each of these systems how long it keeps copies.
In 4.4 the walkthrough also advises asking each cloud and software provider what they keep for you. The same answer shows where copies of your data sit that your deletion concept must cover.

In the business continuity plan from 4.2, the “Recovery” section puts a system back into use only once it has been checked. Add under “Further rules” that this check includes working through the erasure list again.
An assistant can fill in 4.4, and you check and finish the item. The walkthrough has no screen for the deletion concept itself.
walk.seeItAlt: The start page of the NIS 2 walkthrough: on the left “You are in the right place.” with four cards, on the right “Your path” with the first items from “Register with your authority” to “Know how to report an incident”. The first three are done and “Write down what your company has” is started

items.q: How long can personal data be kept?
items.a: As long as it is necessary for its purpose (Art. 5(1)(e)). Where a law requires longer retention, such as § 257 HGB in Germany with six, eight or ten years depending on the document, the exception in Art. 17(3)(b) applies for that period. After that, the data is erased.

items.q: What is the difference between erasure and restriction?
items.a: Erasure makes data unrecognisable, so that no person can be identified from it (SDM building block 60). Restriction of processing (Art. 18) keeps the data stored but allows only narrowly limited processing. In Germany, § 35 BDSG lets restriction take the place of erasure in some cases, such as contractual retention periods; the DSK reads these rules narrowly.

items.q: Is there a DIN or ISO standard for a deletion concept?
items.a: The German standard DIN 66398 of 2016, “Leitlinie zur Entwicklung eines Löschkonzepts mit Ableitung von Löschfristen für personenbezogene Daten”, is withdrawn according to DIN Media and replaced by DIN EN ISO/IEC 27555:2025-09, “Guidelines on personally identifiable information deletion”. Both are paid documents, so we do not reproduce their content. The GDPR prescribes no standard.

items.q: What do you do when someone asks for their data to be erased?
items.a: Check whether a ground in Art. 17(1) applies and no exception in paragraph 3. Inform the person without undue delay and in any event within one month; for complex or numerous requests the period can be extended by two months (Art. 12(3)). Erase at processors too, inform recipients (Art. 19) and record that the erasure was done.

meta.title: GDPR compliant: what your company has to be able to prove
meta.description: GDPR compliant means you keep to the principles in Art. 5 and can prove it. Which records carry that proof, and why a seal does not take the duty off you.

compliant.title: GDPR compliant: what your company has to be able to demonstrate
compliant.subtitle: The GDPR asks two things: your company complies with the principles in Art. 5(1), and it can demonstrate that (Art. 5(2), accountability). To do so it takes measures that fit its processing and the risks involved, and keeps them up to date (Art. 24(1)). The proof rests on records such as the record of processing, the TOMs and the contracts.

sections.heading: What does GDPR compliant mean?
paragraphs: The word does not appear in the GDPR. What it means is what Art. 5 requires: personal data is processed according to six principles, and the controller is responsible for complying with them and must be able to demonstrate it.
The principles in Art. 5(1) are lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality.
Paragraph 2 calls the duty to demonstrate accountability. Complying and proving it therefore go together: when your company is asked, it shows how it puts the principles into practice.

sections.heading: What Art. 24 asks of your company
paragraphs: Art. 24(1) turns this into a duty to act. The controller implements appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that processing complies with the GDPR and to be able to demonstrate it. What is appropriate depends on the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing and on the risks to people's rights and freedoms.

The measures are reviewed and updated where necessary. Where proportionate to the processing, they include appropriate data protection policies (paragraph 2); the German text says “Datenschutzvorkehrungen”, in our reading written rules either way.

For a company with 50 to 250 staff this means, in our reading: records for what you actually process, as detailed as the risk requires. Payroll needs different safeguards from tracking employees' locations.

sections.heading: Which records carry the proof
paragraphs: The record of processing activities shows what you process and why, and you make it available to the supervisory authority on request (Art. 30(1) and (4)). The TOMs describe how you protect the data (Art. 32). Data processing agreements show that your service providers are bound (Art. 28).

Where a data protection impact assessment is required, it belongs here too (Art. 35). You document personal data breaches with the facts, effects and remedial action, by the wording including those you do not have to notify (Art. 33(5)). Where processing is based on consent, you must be able to demonstrate the consent (Art. 7(1)).
We cover the record of processing, TOMs, DPAs, the DPIA and data breaches in an article each.
sections.law: Art. 7(1) · Art. 28 · Art. 30 · Art. 32 · Art. 33(5) · Art. 35 GDPR

sections.heading: An example: the authority asks
paragraphs: Lenz Kunststofftechnik GmbH (made up, 160 staff) gets a letter from the data protection authority of its federal state. A former applicant has complained that his documents are still stored. The authority wants to know how Lenz handles applicant data.

Lenz produces the entry “Applications” from its record of processing with purpose and erasure period, the DPA with the vendor of its applicant portal, and the TOMs for the portal. The company adds the log of the last deletion run.

Had the erasure period only been in its privacy notice, Lenz could have named it but not proven that it is kept. That is exactly the difference Art. 5(2) makes, here for the principle of storage limitation (paragraph 1(e)).

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Relying on a seal or on a vendor's claim. A certification under Art. 42 relates to processing operations and does not reduce your responsibility (paragraphs 1 and 4). The GDPR's obligations fall on controllers and processors. Whether a piece of software fits depends on how you use it.
Writing the records once and leaving them. Art. 24(1) requires the measures to be reviewed and updated where necessary; an old record proves an old state.

Taking the exemption for organisations with fewer than 250 employees as a general one. It concerns the record of processing and falls away once a processing is not occasional, such as the monthly payroll (Art. 30(5)).

sections.heading: With an AI assistant
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot can build an overview from the records you already have: which proof exists, which is missing and which is out of date, sorted by the principles in Art. 5(1). It can draft missing entries and prepare a reply to the authority.

Whether a measure is appropriate and what you send the authority is your company's decision. In our reading, a draft becomes proof only once you have checked it and adopted it. Whatever you show the assistant, its vendor processes too; settle first under which agreement that happens.
The NIS 2 walkthrough on nisd2.eu does not cover the GDPR. A GDPR walkthrough on nisd2.eu is in the works, with the same MCP server as the NIS 2 walkthrough.

items.q: Is there an official GDPR certificate?
items.a: The GDPR provides for voluntary certification mechanisms and data protection seals and marks (Art. 42(1) and (3)). They relate to processing operations. A certification can help demonstrate that you meet your obligations (Art. 24(3)), but it does not reduce your responsibility (Art. 42(4)).

items.q: From how many employees does the GDPR apply?
items.a: The GDPR has no minimum size: it applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by automated means and to structured paper files (Art. 2(1)). Some obligations have thresholds, such as the record of processing (Art. 30(5)). In Germany your company needs a data protection officer if it constantly employs as a rule at least 20 persons dealing with the automated processing of personal data (§ 38(1) BDSG).

items.q: Is a data protection officer enough to be GDPR compliant?
items.a: No. The data protection officer informs, advises and monitors (Art. 39(1)). Your company remains responsible for compliance and for demonstrating it (Art. 5(2), Art. 24(1)).

items.q: What belongs in a GDPR checklist?
items.a: A checklist helps if it asks about your own processing. For each one, go through the six principles in Art. 5(1) and note which record shows that you comply. Where no record is listed, there is a gap in your proof.

items.q: Who checks whether a company is GDPR compliant?
items.a: The data protection authority; for companies in Germany, the authority of the federal state (§ 40(1) BDSG). It can order you to provide any information it needs for its tasks (Art. 58(1)(a)), and your company cooperates with it on request (Art. 31).

meta.title: Privacy management software: what to look for under GDPR
meta.description: What privacy management software should do for Art. 5(2) and Art. 24 GDPR: records of processing, TOMs, contracts, requests, breaches and evidence.

dpms.title: Privacy management software: what matters
dpms.subtitle: Privacy management software keeps the records your company uses to demonstrate that it complies with the GDPR: the record of processing, TOMs, contracts with processors, data subject requests and personal data breaches. No law requires it. When buying, look for visible deadlines, a change history and a complete export.

sections.heading: What is a privacy management system?
paragraphs: The term does not appear in the GDPR. It means the way your company organises its GDPR obligations and the evidence for them. At its core is accountability: the controller is responsible for compliance with the principles and must “be able to demonstrate compliance” (Art. 5(2)).

Art. 24(1) requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and be able to demonstrate that processing complies with the GDPR. Those measures are reviewed and updated where necessary. Where proportionate, they include appropriate data protection policies (para. 2).
Software is one possible tool for this; the law requires none in particular. The record of processing activities, for example, is kept in writing, which includes electronic form (Art. 30(3)).

sections.heading: Which obligations should the software cover?
paragraphs: The DSK is the conference of Germany's data protection authorities. In its action plan for companies (Kurzpapier Nr. 8) it lists documentation duties that belong to accountability: the record of processing (Art. 30), the documentation of personal data breaches (Art. 33(5)) and of instructions to processors (Art. 28(3)(a)).

For a company with 50 to 250 staff, that means in daily practice: a record of processing activities, a description of TOMs under Art. 32, contracts with processors under Art. 28, data subject requests under Art. 15 to 22, and a breach log. Where a data protection impact assessment is needed, its documentation comes on top (Art. 35(7)).

Two deadlines should be visible in the software. You answer data subject requests without undue delay and in any event within one month, extendable for complex or numerous requests (Art. 12(3)). You notify a reportable breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours (Art. 33(1)).
sections.law: Art. 12(3) · Art. 28 · Art. 30 · Art. 33 · Art. 35(7) GDPR

sections.heading: What to look for when buying
paragraphs: The software should follow the required contents of Art. 30(1) and link entries: a service provider, its contract under Art. 28 and the activities it works on. Then you enter a change only once.
It should record who changed what and when. For the record of processing, the DSK recommends documenting changes and keeping that documentation for one year.
Your external data protection officer needs access, auditors need read access. All data should export in an open format, so you can switch vendors without losing records.

The software itself holds personal data, such as data subject requests and breaches. If the vendor runs it for you, it processes that data on your behalf: check the contract under Art. 28(3), where the data is stored and which sub-processors are involved.

sections.heading: Example: choosing with a real case
paragraphs: Muster Metall GmbH, a made-up company with 80 employees and an external data protection officer, keeps its record of processing in a spreadsheet so far. Contracts sit in a folder, requests in the management mailbox.

In two trial accounts it runs through a case it actually had last year: an access request from a former employee. It checks whether the software shows the deadline, which entries in the record are affected, and whether the reply can be filed with its date.
Finally it exports everything and opens the file. Software whose data cannot be exported completely is ruled out.

sections.heading: Which mistakes to avoid when buying
paragraphs: Do not buy software before someone in the company is responsible. Without a person who maintains the entries, it stays empty.
Do not expect the software to fulfil obligations. It records what your company decided and did, and its templates describe another business until you adapt them.
Do not decide without your data protection officer. They should be able to carry out their tasks under Art. 39 with it, such as monitoring compliance.

sections.heading: With an AI assistant: what the software should offer
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot can draft entries for the record of processing, compare contracts with the points in Art. 28(3) and structure a data protection impact assessment along Art. 35(7). If the software offers an MCP server, an interface following the open Model Context Protocol, the assistant reads and writes in it directly.

Then ask what the assistant may do there: read, write, delete as well? And whether each entry shows that an assistant wrote it. Purposes, time limits and notifications remain your company's decisions as controller.

Whatever the assistant reads, its vendor processes too. Where the vendor acts as a processor, a contract under Art. 28(3) is required with it as well. A GDPR walkthrough on nisd2.eu is in the works, with the same MCP server as the NIS 2 walkthrough.

items.q: Is privacy management software mandatory?
items.a: No. The GDPR requires that you can demonstrate compliance (Art. 5(2)) and, for the record of processing, written form, which can be electronic (Art. 30(3)). It does not prescribe any particular software.

items.q: Is a spreadsheet enough for GDPR records?
items.a: For the record of processing, a spreadsheet can meet the written form, and the DSK itself publishes a template. It gets harder with deadlines, links between contracts and activities, and the question of who changed what and when. That is where comparing software pays off.

items.q: Does software replace the data protection officer?
items.a: No. Whether you must designate one is set by Art. 37 GDPR and, in Germany, by § 38(1) BDSG, for example where you as a rule constantly employ at least 20 persons in the automated processing of personal data. Software can support the officer, but a person is designated.

items.q: Privacy management and an ISMS: do you need both?
items.a: An ISMS (information security management system) protects your company's information and systems, for example for your NIS 2 obligations. Privacy management asks about the risk to the people whose data you process. The DSK calls the record of processing an essential element of a comprehensive management system for data protection and information security; some records overlap, such as the TOMs.
